chunks: Spectrum of a square wave and pulse train. The question: Draw spectral content of square wave/pulse train.
A repeating pulse has a line spectrum: separate lines at the repeat frequency and its whole-number multiples, plus a line at zero frequency (DC) equal to the average.
The line heights follow a smooth, wavy outline set by the pulse width. Wherever that outline touches zero, a line disappears.
So a 50% square wave has only odd lines, and narrow pulses spread energy to high frequencies.
Picture a piano where only the keys at multiples of a base note are played. How loud each key sounds follows a smooth wavy outline drawn over the keyboard.
Where the outline touches zero, those keys are silent. Change the pulse width and the outline stretches, so different keys fall silent.
Lines sit at n equals 1 3 5 with heights 0. 637 0. 212 0. 127 volts. The dashed sinc envelope has its first null at n equals 2 , so every even line lands on a zero.
The DC line (0. 5 volts) is the average.
Line spectrum: a spectrum made of separate lines, as for any repeating signal. Harmonic: a multiple of the repeat frequency.
Envelope: the smooth outline that the line heights follow. Null: a frequency where the envelope is zero, so the line there vanishes.
Duty cycle: the fraction of each period the pulse is high. Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from low to high.
Take a 0 to 1 volts pulse train with duty cycle D. At D = 50%, the even harmonics are zero and the odd ones are 0. 64 volts, 0. 21 volts and 0. 13 volts.
At D = 25%, the DC line is 0. 25 volts, the first lines are 0. 45 volts, 0. 32 volts and 0. 15 volts, and the 4th harmonic is zero.
In general, nulls fall at every harmonic number that is a multiple of 1 ÷ D. Real edges add a second outline: above a knee near 1 ÷ (π times rise time), the lines fall faster.
For a 1 nanoseconds edge that knee is about 318 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"A periodic pulse train has a line spectrum: a DC line equal to the average, then lines at multiples of the repetition frequency.
The line heights follow a sinc envelope set by the pulse width, with the nth harmonic equal to 2 volts times sine of n pi D over n pi.
Nulls fall at multiples of f0 over D, so a 50% square wave has only odd harmonics falling as 1 over n, and 25% duty loses every fourth.
Finite rise time adds a second sinc, so the lines drop at 40 decibels per decade above about 1 over pi times the rise time."
